questions.prompt: Why spread a database across multiple resources?
options: To improve performance and availability
Only to increase capacity, with no possible improvement in throughput
To eliminate transaction-coordination costs entirely
To guarantee a linear reduction in latency for every query
questions.explanation: Distributing resources can improve performance and availability; it does not eliminate the need for coordination or transactions.

questions.prompt: Under the lecture's assumptions, what is the main difference between parallel and distributed DBMSs?
options: Parallel DBMSs use shared RAM in every architecture
The distance between nodes and the cost of communication
Distributed DBMSs cannot provide a unified SQL interface
Parallel DBMSs do not need concurrency control
questions.explanation: Parallel-system nodes are usually close together and connected by a fast LAN; distributed systems must account for network costs and failures.

questions.prompt: What should happen when an SQL query moves from a single node to a multi-node cluster?
options: One extra result row should automatically be added for each replica
The application should have to UNION all shards itself
Its logical result should remain unchanged
Rows on slow-responding nodes may be omitted
questions.explanation: Data independence requires the same semantics when physical placement changes; replication must not duplicate query results.

questions.prompt: What must a cluster spanning several continents pay particular attention to?
options: Minimizing local I/O alone, because the network has no effect
Assuming network latency is always lower than RAM-access latency
Counting CPU costs alone and ignoring data transfers between nodes
Communication costs and failures
questions.explanation: The lecture emphasizes that communication in a distributed system cannot be assumed to be cheap or failure-free.

questions.prompt: What does increasing throughput most closely mean?
options: Completing more queries per unit of time
Reducing the time for exactly one query, regardless of the total workload
Increasing the number of waiting queries without completing more
Returning fewer rows to finish the same query faster
questions.explanation: Throughput measures the rate at which work is completed; latency measures how long an individual query takes.

questions.prompt: In a shared-memory architecture, what resource do multiple CPUs access in common?
options: A memory address space
Each CPU has private RAM and shares only disk storage
Each CPU has entirely private RAM and disk storage
Only metadata is shared; all RAM holding data is private
questions.explanation: The CPUs share memory through a fast interconnect; private-memory descriptions refer to other architectures.

questions.prompt: What direct advantage follows from processors sharing one memory address space?
options: Each instance can operate without coordinating with other instances
CPUs have a common view of in-memory structures
Adding CPUs guarantees unlimited linear speedup
All data access must use network messages between nodes
questions.explanation: Processors can see common in-memory structures and coordinate through them. Shared bandwidth and synchronization can still bottleneck execution; common visibility does not remove concurrent-access rules.

questions.prompt: What does the system architecture determine directly?
options: The same SQL query must return different logical results depending on the RAM configuration
Every partition must contain the same complete copy
Which shared resources the CPUs can access
Every join must use one fixed algorithm
questions.explanation: The architecture determines resource sharing and coordination, rather than dictating the schema or the number of result rows.

questions.prompt: Can an instance in a shared-memory system ignore the existence of the other instances?
options: Yes, because shared addresses automatically guarantee isolation
Yes, every RAM access is automatically an atomic transaction
Yes, because concurrent access occurs only in shared-nothing systems
No, instances must coordinate access to shared structures
questions.explanation: Shared RAM makes communication easier but does not automatically make concurrent operations correct; the slide says instances must be aware of one another.

questions.prompt: Why is shared memory also called shared everything in this lecture?
options: CPUs can share both the address space and the storage layer in the illustrated model
Every node has completely private RAM and disk storage
Only disks are shared, while all address spaces are private
Each CPU must hold an independent copy of the entire database
questions.explanation: The shared-memory diagram shows shared memory and storage, whereas shared disk shares only the storage layer.

questions.prompt: Which architecture gives each CPU private memory while allowing access to a common logical disk?
options: Shared disk
Shared memory with all RAM shared
Shared nothing with private storage at each node
Shared memory in which CPUs do not share an address space
questions.explanation: Shared disk separates the CPUs' RAM but shares storage. Shared memory shares an address space, while shared nothing uses both private RAM and private disks.

questions.prompt: What bottleneck is identified when a shared-disk system has many CPUs?
options: Having to repartition every table after every read
The shared disk
Every CPU must wait for the same database-wide lock for every query
CPUs cannot read data without first holding a private copy of the entire database
questions.explanation: Many CPUs place load on the same disk; private RAM does not remove the storage bottleneck.

questions.prompt: Which architecture lets nodes with private RAM add execution capacity while using the same logical storage layer?
options: Only shared nothing, because shared disk requires CPU and disk capacity to grow together
Only shared memory, because shared disk cannot separate the execution layer
Shared disk
No architecture allows compute and storage capacity to grow separately
questions.explanation: Shared disk separates private execution memory from common storage. Adding an execution node need not add a separate logical database, but storage contention and cache coordination remain costs.

questions.prompt: Which statement best matches the three architecture diagrams?
options: Shared disk shares all RAM between CPUs
Shared nothing lets a CPU directly access another node's disk
Shared memory gives each CPU a separate memory address space
Shared disk and shared nothing both give each node private RAM
questions.explanation: Both models show private RAM; their difference is whether disks are shared or private.

questions.prompt: What is a correct implication of private memory in a shared-disk system?
options: CPUs must still coordinate access to shared data; a shared disk does not replace concurrency control
Each CPU always immediately sees every change in another CPU's RAM
A single shared disk makes concurrent writes impossible
Each CPU must store a separate logical database on a different disk
questions.explanation: Shared disk shares storage but keeps RAM private. Having one on-disk copy does not automatically eliminate all contention.

questions.prompt: A node has its own CPU, RAM, and disk and communicates with other nodes only through the network. What architecture is this?
options: Shared nothing
Shared memory, because the nodes still exchange messages
Shared disk, because all nodes query one logical database
Shared memory with a private cache for each CPU
questions.explanation: Shared nothing does not directly share RAM or disks between nodes; pipelining, by contrast, is an execution technique.

questions.prompt: Why can consistency be harder to maintain in a shared-nothing system?
options: Instances access the same RAM addresses directly without locks
Nodes must coordinate over the network
All nodes modify a single shared buffer pool
Each node must use the same physical disk
questions.explanation: Independent resources help the system scale, but maintaining consistency requires network messages.

questions.prompt: What is the natural way to increase capacity in a shared-nothing system?
options: Add only CPUs that access an existing node's RAM and disk
Replace all private disks with a single shared disk
Add nodes with their own CPUs, RAM, and disks
Only replicate data without adding computing resources
questions.explanation: Adding nodes adds independent resources; sharing disks would introduce the trade-offs of a shared-disk architecture.

questions.prompt: In a shared-nothing system, how does node A obtain data held only at node B?
options: Directly access B's RAM through a shared address space
Read the cluster's shared disk directly
Use A's cache, which is guaranteed to contain every tuple at B
Communicate with B over the network or transfer the relevant data
questions.explanation: Nodes communicate only through the network; they do not directly share RAM or disks as the other architectures do.

questions.prompt: Which deployment trade-off fits a shared-nothing architecture?
options: Commodity resources are easy to add, but coordination software is more complex
Hardware is always the most expensive, but network communication is unnecessary
Capacity cannot be increased by adding nodes
All nodes share memory, so consistency is automatically guaranteed
questions.explanation: Independent resources make scale-out convenient, but the system must handle network coordination and consistency.

questions.prompt: Running two customers' queries at the same time is which type of parallelism?
options: Intra-operator, because the same operator type may appear in both queries
Inter-operator within a single query
Inter-query
Partition parallelism for a single scan
questions.explanation: Inter-query parallelism runs different queries concurrently; intra-operator parallelism divides the work of one operator.

questions.prompt: Multiple CPUs scan different parts of a table for one query. What type of parallelism is this?
options: Inter-query, because each CPU counts as a separate query
Only inter-operator, because there are multiple CPUs
Only pipeline parallelism, even though the data for just one operator is divided
Intra-query, intra-operator
questions.explanation: A single scan is divided among several CPUs, so this is parallelism within one operator of the same query.

questions.prompt: What is one direct goal of intra-query parallelism?
options: Reducing the latency of long-running queries
Only increasing the number of concurrent users, with no possible reduction in one query's runtime
Guaranteeing that throughput always increases exactly in proportion to the CPU count
Eliminating all waiting time between operators
questions.explanation: Dividing the work can shorten query execution time; concurrency control is still necessary.

questions.prompt: In a pipeline from f to g to h, different operators process different tuples simultaneously. What is this?
options: Inter-query parallelism, because each tuple counts as a query
Inter-operator parallelism
Only intra-operator parallelism, because the operators process different tuples
Only bushy parallelism, because every pipeline consists of independent branches
questions.explanation: Operator stages overlap within the same query; these are not independent queries.

questions.prompt: Two independent join branches of a plan tree execute concurrently. What does this illustrate?
options: Intra-operator parallelism, because both joins have the same operator name
Inter-query parallelism, because the branches are always separate SQL statements
Bushy (tree) parallelism
A linear pipeline, because the left branch's output must be the right branch's input
questions.explanation: Bushy parallelism exploits independent branches; it does not require all operators to run one after another.

questions.prompt: What distinguishes partition parallelism in the diagram from pipelining?
options: Multiple independent queries share one partition
Different operators execute only sequentially over all the data
Every CPU repeats the same operation over the entire input
Multiple instances of the same operator process different portions of the data
questions.explanation: Partition parallelism divides the input to one operator; pipelining overlaps different operators.

questions.prompt: What mechanism requires attention when more queries run concurrently?
options: Concurrency control that accounts for parallelism
Only output-order control, with no control over shared data
Isolation can be discarded because the queries run on different CPUs
Only metadata needs locking; all data accesses are always independent
questions.explanation: The lecture notes that inter-query parallelism needs appropriate concurrency control; isolation cannot simply be discarded.

questions.prompt: In a two-branch join tree with materialization before the root join, what constrains the root join?
options: Having multiple CPUs eliminates all input dependencies
It must wait for its inputs to be materialized as required by the plan
It can produce the complete result before either branch produces data
It must serialize both independent branches
questions.explanation: Materialization creates a dependency: the root join needs the relevant inputs. The two lower branches can still execute concurrently.

questions.prompt: An operator must receive all its input before producing any output. What does this blocking behavior most directly affect?
options: It completely eliminates the ability to parallelize the input scan
It increases the required number of replicas for every table
The ability to overlap its execution with a downstream operator in a pipeline
It forces every upstream operator to use the same CPU
questions.explanation: Pipelining depends on forwarding results while they are being produced; materialization can interrupt that overlap.

questions.prompt: A query uses both a partitioned scan and a pipeline into a filter. Which statement is correct?
options: These two types of parallelism are mutually exclusive within a query
With multiple CPUs, the only possible classification is inter-query
Pipelining requires each operator to process the entire input sequentially
Intra-operator and inter-operator parallelism can be combined
questions.explanation: Both levels can coexist: work is divided within an operator, and execution overlaps between operators.

questions.prompt: How does horizontal partitioning divide a table?
options: It divides each tuple's attributes into groups of columns
It copies the entire table to every node
It keeps all rows on one node and divides only the index
It divides tuples into disjoint subsets
questions.explanation: Horizontal partitioning divides rows while retaining their columns; dividing columns is vertical partitioning.

questions.prompt: After executing query fragments on the partitions, what must the DBMS do?
options: Combine their results into one answer
Return only the result of the partition with the most rows
Return replicas as additional logical rows
Always apply DISTINCT, even when the query uses bag semantics
questions.explanation: Physical partitioning must still produce the complete result of the logical query.

questions.prompt: What is another name for database partitioning?
options: Replication
Sharding
Vertical projection
Materialization
questions.explanation: Sharding refers to partitioning data; it is distinct from backup or lock management.

questions.prompt: Besides data size, what should be considered when choosing a partitioning column?
options: Only the row count, because every tuple costs the same to process
Only disk capacity, ignoring access frequency
Load and data-usage patterns
Only key order, because all workload distributions are equivalent
questions.explanation: Balanced row counts do not guarantee balanced load; the lecture identifies size, load, and usage as considerations.

questions.prompt: Which option is not one of the three horizontal-partitioning methods discussed?
options: Round-robin distribution of whole tuples in turn
Hash partitioning that maps whole tuples using a key
Range partitioning that divides tuples by key ranges
Separating personal-information columns from payment-information columns
questions.explanation: Dividing columns is vertical partitioning; all three methods in the slides distribute whole tuples.

questions.prompt: With 4 partitions P1–P4 and distribution starting at P1, where does the 6th tuple go?
options: P2
P1, because each cycle restarts after the 5th tuple
P3, because the 6th tuple has index 6 mod 3
P4, because the four partitions receive consecutive pairs of tuples
questions.explanation: The sequence repeats as P1,P2,P3,P4,P1,P2; placement does not depend on key values.

questions.prompt: What is a direct strength of round-robin partitioning?
options: It puts all equal join keys on the same node
It distributes tuple counts relatively evenly
It routes range queries using only key values
It guarantees balanced CPU costs even when tuples have different processing costs
questions.explanation: Taking turns balances row counts, but it does not guarantee placement based on key values.

questions.prompt: Does round-robin partitioning guarantee that two tuples with the same key are in the same partition?
options: Yes, because round-robin uses the hash of the key
Yes, because duplicate values are always grouped before distribution
No, placement depends on the distribution turn
Yes, provided the tuples belong to the same table
questions.explanation: Round-robin does not use key values, so equal keys can be spread across multiple nodes.

questions.prompt: There are 10 tuples and 3 partitions, starting at P1. What are the respective tuple counts?
questions.explanation: Turns 1,4,7,10 go to P1; 2,5,8 go to P2; and 3,6,9 go to P3. Because distribution starts at P1, that partition receives the extra tuple.

questions.prompt: Why do balanced tuple counts not guarantee balanced processing costs?
options: Tuples can differ in size or processing cost
Round-robin always sends every hot key to one node
Balanced tuple counts force every partition to have the same byte count
Every partition must have the same access frequency
questions.explanation: Round-robin balances counts; it does not automatically balance every kind of cost or the popularity of the data.

questions.prompt: Which query is best suited to hash partitioning on customer_id?
options: WHERE customer_id BETWEEN 10 AND 90, guaranteeing that only one shard is read
WHERE customer_id = 42
ORDER BY customer_id, so partitions can be concatenated without merging
WHERE email = a value, when email is not the partition key
questions.explanation: An equality lookup on the key identifies the partition; a range of key values usually does not correspond to a range of hash buckets.

questions.prompt: Where do tuples with the same key value go when the same partitioning function is used?
options: Different partitions to avoid duplicate keys
Every partition, because hashing always creates replicas
The same partition
Whichever partition is least busy, regardless of the hash value
questions.explanation: A deterministic function maps equal keys to the same destination; this does not mean it automatically balances the current load.

questions.prompt: With partition index = h(k) mod 4 and h(k)=14, what is the index?
questions.explanation: Dividing 14 by 4 leaves a remainder of 2. This is an index, not a partition name P using numbering that starts at 1.

questions.prompt: Why does hash partitioning help GROUP BY on the partition key itself?
options: Rows in the same group can be placed on the same node
The hash function has already computed SUM for each group
Each group always contains only one tuple
Different values can never share a hash bucket
questions.explanation: Co-locating a group's data enables local processing; hashing does not replace the aggregate operation.

questions.prompt: What problem can arise if one key appears in 70% of the rows?
options: Hashing guarantees that the hot key is spread evenly across all nodes
Skew can overload one partition
Each row with the hot key automatically becomes a separate logical group
Every query on that key reads only one row
questions.explanation: Hashing sends equal keys to the same destination, so a hot key can still cause an uneven workload.

questions.prompt: P1 contains [a–c], P2 contains [d–e], P3 contains [f–m], and P4 contains [n–z]. Where does key h belong?
options: P1
P2
P3
P4
questions.explanation: h lies in the range f–m; routing follows range boundaries, not insertion order.

questions.prompt: Which type of query is an additional strength of range partitioning over hash partitioning?
options: Every lookup on a non-partition-key column reads only one node
Every GROUP BY on another column is entirely local
Every range contains the same number of rows without using statistics
Range queries on the partition key
questions.explanation: Consecutive key values map to identifiable partitions; hashing does not preserve this order.

questions.prompt: How should range boundaries be defined so that partitions are disjoint subsets that cover the stored data?
options: They should not overlap and should cover the domain to be stored
Every range should cover the entire domain so nothing is missed
Ranges may overlap arbitrarily without a destination-selection rule
Non-overlap alone is enough; not every valid value needs to be covered
questions.explanation: Boundary rules must assign each tuple to exactly one partition; overlapping ranges create ambiguity.

questions.prompt: What problem can arise if most data falls within one range?
options: Range partitioning automatically balances row counts regardless of the distribution
That partition becomes larger and slower to process
Duplicate keys are automatically spread evenly across all ranges
Only hash partitioning can suffer from skew
questions.explanation: Ranges do not automatically contain equal numbers of rows; a skewed distribution can create a bottleneck.

questions.prompt: Which partitions in the diagram must be read for keys from g to k?
options: P1 [a–c] and P2 [d–e]
All four partitions, even though their boundaries are known
Only P3 [f–m]
Only P4 [n–z]
questions.explanation: The entire range g–k lies inside f–m, so the other partitions can be pruned.

questions.prompt: What is the main goal of replication identified in the lecture?
options: Guaranteeing that every write is cheaper than with a single copy
Eliminating the need to transmit updates between nodes
Increasing logical capacity without increasing physical storage
Increasing availability
questions.explanation: Multiple copies can keep data available when one location cannot serve it.

questions.prompt: What does partition replication mean?
options: Keeping copies of an entire partition in multiple locations
Dividing one partition into disjoint sets of tuples
Storing the whole table in every partition, regardless of how many partitions it has
Storing each column of a partition in a different location
questions.explanation: Copying a partition is different from table replication, which copies an entire table.

questions.prompt: A complete table will be copied to every worker for local joins. Which table is generally the most suitable candidate?
options: A very large, constantly updated table, because synchronization is always free
A small, read-only table
A table that occupies most of the storage but is rarely read
A table requiring every write to synchronize with thousands of replicas at minimal latency
questions.explanation: A small, read-only table is cheap to copy and creates little update-propagation work. Replicating a very large or rapidly changing table consumes more memory, network capacity and coordination.

questions.prompt: When a table with multiple replicas is updated, what must the DBMS do?
options: Update only one replica and assume the others are always correct
Discard every update after the first replica receives it
Propagate changes to the copies
Let each replica choose a value without synchronization rules
questions.explanation: The lecture requires update propagation for both replication types; the other copies cannot simply be ignored.

questions.prompt: What is the fundamental difference between partitioning and replication?
options: Both create a complete copy at every node
Replication divides a tuple's columns among nodes
Partitioning always creates multiple copies of each tuple
Partitioning divides data; replication creates additional copies
questions.explanation: A system can combine both techniques, but dividing data and copying it serve different purposes.

questions.prompt: What does data transparency allow users to avoid knowing?
options: Where data is located and how it is partitioned and replicated
The names and meanings of tables in the logical schema
The JOIN conditions required by a business query
Which columns a query should return
questions.explanation: Transparency hides physical organization, not the logical meaning of a query.

questions.prompt: How should moving a partition to another node affect an application's SQL?
options: Every SELECT must be edited to include the new node's address
The logical SQL should continue to work as before
The logical result must change with the physical location
Every join between partitions must be removed
questions.explanation: Data transparency preserves the interface and semantics when data placement changes.

questions.prompt: A row has three replicas. Should a logical SELECT automatically return that row three times?
options: Yes, each replica is always an additional logical tuple
Yes, unless the application selects a replica by IP address
No, replicas do not automatically multiply logical results
Only if the DBMS does not automatically apply DISTINCT to every query
questions.explanation: Replication is a physical implementation detail; the result must be equivalent to querying one logical database.

questions.prompt: Who determines which nodes to access when data transparency is maintained?
options: The application must send each query fragment to each machine itself
The user must choose a replica for each row
Every SQL statement must declare the complete partitioning scheme
The DBMS
questions.explanation: The DBMS hides routing and result-combination decisions from the person writing SQL.

questions.prompt: Which claim does not follow from data transparency?
options: Every query has the same runtime under every data layout
SQL retains the same logical meaning
Users do not need to know where replicas are located
Users do not need to know how tables are partitioned
questions.explanation: Semantic transparency does not guarantee identical performance; data location still affects cost.

questions.prompt: How are the outputs of parallel partition scans basically combined?
options: Always remove duplicates, as in SELECT DISTINCT
Concatenate the result streams
Keep only the fastest partition's result
Compute the Cartesian product of the streams
questions.explanation: A parallel scan combines the outputs of its parts; it does not automatically add DISTINCT or JOIN semantics.

questions.prompt: In the slide's example, a sequential scan takes 200,000 seconds. Ideally, how long does it take on 100 machines?
options: 200 seconds
20,000 seconds
2,000 seconds
200,000 seconds
questions.explanation: 200,000/100=2,000. This is an ideal calculation, not a claim that there is no overhead.

questions.prompt: When can a filter skip an entire site?
options: When the site contains fewer rows than other sites
When the site responds more slowly than in the previous scan
When another site has already returned at least one matching row
When it is known that the site contains no tuple satisfying the condition
questions.explanation: Partition pruning requires establishing that no matching row is present; it is not based on a site's name or speed.

questions.prompt: How does partitioning by date ranges help a query that needs only January?
options: Skip partitions whose date ranges do not overlap January
Read only the partition containing the most January rows
Skip the January partition because the condition already identifies the month
Read one row from each partition to infer the remaining rows
questions.explanation: Range metadata allows sites known to contain no matching data to be excluded.

questions.prompt: What can make the actual speedup lower than the linear speedup in the example?
options: Every partition always takes exactly the same time to scan
Coordination overhead or uneven load across nodes
Adding machines proportionally increases the total amount of logical data
Combining results cannot involve communication or coordination costs
questions.explanation: Ideal speedup ignores overhead and bottlenecks; these reduce performance without making the parallel scan semantically incorrect.

questions.prompt: Data is partitioned using a function of the lookup key. Where should the request go?
options: Every node, because equality lookups always require broadcasting
Only the coordinator, even if the data is elsewhere
The appropriate node identified from the key
The node with the least data rather than the node mapped from the key
questions.explanation: Knowing the key-to-partition mapping allows direct routing and avoids unnecessary broadcasting.

questions.prompt: Without partition-key routing, a directory or another usable lookup mechanism, how can a basic system find a key across all nodes?
options: Choose a random node and interpret an empty result as proof that the row does not exist
Ask only the node with the smallest key
Ask only a replica of an arbitrary partition
Broadcast the request to the nodes
questions.explanation: A broadcast asks every node because any of them could hold the row. Known placement can avoid this fan-out; a matching column name alone does not reveal physical location.

questions.prompt: A table is partitioned by customer_id, but a lookup uses email and there is no secondary index. What follows?
options: A single partition cannot be inferred from the email alone
An email always maps to the same partition as its customer_id
Every shard always has a complete copy of all email values
An equality lookup automatically has a global secondary index
questions.explanation: The lookup key differs from the partition key, so routing information is missing; all nodes may need to be queried.

questions.prompt: When can both range and hash partitioning help with a key lookup?
options: Only when each node has a complete copy of the table
When the partitioning scheme uses the key being looked up
Only when all data has been sorted on one machine
Even when the lookup key is entirely unrelated to the partition key
questions.explanation: Both schemes can map a specific key to a partition; full replication is not required.

questions.prompt: There are 8 nodes, and the key's partition is known. What is the direct advantage over broadcasting?
options: Reducing the physical size of each row to 1/8
Guaranteeing that the lookup needs no memory or disk access
Reducing the number of nodes that receive the lookup request
Eliminating all transaction-coordination costs
questions.explanation: Routing reduces communication fan-out; it does not automatically change data size or hardware durability.

questions.prompt: What is the role of h_n in parallel hashing?
options: Establishing a global ascending order across nodes
Performing the local hash join in place of all later steps
Selecting only a bucket in the coordinator's RAM
Distributing data among nodes
questions.explanation: h_n divides data among nodes; local hashing steps follow afterward.

questions.prompt: After distribution using h_n, what does each node do?
options: Perform external hashing independently
Always gather all data at the coordinator for hashing
Perform a mandatory global sort before any hashing step
Keep only the tuple with the smallest hash on each machine
questions.explanation: Inter-node distribution is combined with a local external-hashing algorithm.

questions.prompt: Why does the slide compare parallel hashing with recursive partitioning?
options: No step needs to store intermediate partitions
An inter-node partitioning step is followed by further partitioning or processing within each node
Every level must use a single bucket
All data must fit in one node's RAM
questions.explanation: This hierarchy of data subdivision resembles recursive partitioning; it does not require all data to fit in memory.

questions.prompt: What can happen if h_n sends most tuples to one node?
options: Lightly loaded nodes automatically receive the data without repartitioning
Adding nodes automatically guarantees perfectly balanced redistribution
That node can dominate the completion time
Completion time depends only on the fastest node
questions.explanation: Skew reduces the benefit of dividing the work; hash partitioning does not guarantee perfectly balanced load.

questions.prompt: Which statement about inter-node and local hashing is correct?
options: h_n replaces all local partitioning, even when data exceeds RAM
Inter-node hashing must preserve global key order
Using hashing at every level makes collisions impossible
They divide data at different levels
questions.explanation: The diagram distinguishes h_n from the local h_p and h_r steps; one level does not replace the entire algorithm.

questions.prompt: On which attribute must two relations be hash-partitioned to perform an equijoin locally?
options: The join key
Their existing partition keys, even if these differ from the join key
Two independently chosen columns in the two tables
Each tuple's position within its table
questions.explanation: Partitioning on the join key brings potentially matching tuples to the same node; partitioning on another column can miss pairs.

questions.prompt: R and S use incompatible key-to-node mappings. What is the risk?
options: Matching tuples are still guaranteed to be together because the key names match
Matching tuples may be on different nodes
Hash join finds all tuples on other nodes without network communication
Equal partition counts alone always guarantee co-location
questions.explanation: Co-location requires compatible mappings for both inputs.

questions.prompt: What happens in phase 2 of a parallel hash join?
options: Both relations are gathered onto one node immediately after being distributed
Both relations must be globally sorted
A local hash join runs at each node
The two inputs are merely concatenated without checking join keys
questions.explanation: After repartitioning, each node uses a conventional hash-join algorithm, such as Grace hash join.

questions.prompt: R has a tuple with key 7 at node A, and S has a tuple with key 7 at node B. What must the distribution phase ensure?
options: Preserve their locations and join only tuples already present locally
Send only the keys, discarding all attributes needed in the result
Change key values so the two nodes have disjoint key domains
Bring both tuples to the same destination node
questions.explanation: The goal is to co-locate matching pairs; data must not be changed or deleted simply to avoid communication.

questions.prompt: What important extra cost does parallel hash join incur compared with a single-node hash join?
options: Transferring data between nodes during repartitioning
A mandatory global sort despite using hash join
Eliminating all local I/O even when partitions exceed RAM
A mandatory complete copy of both tables at every node
questions.explanation: Parallel hash join adds a network-distribution phase before the local joins.

questions.prompt: To concatenate locally sorted outputs directly into one global ordering, how should keys be distributed?
options: Round-robin, after which any concatenation of outputs gives global order
Range partitioning
Full replication on every machine so each tuple is sorted repeatedly
Hash partitioning, after which concatenating buckets in hash order is sufficient
questions.explanation: Disjoint ordered key ranges ensure every key in an earlier partition precedes those in later partitions. Hash destinations do not establish that ordering, even after each destination sorts locally.

questions.prompt: After range partitioning, what does each machine do?
options: Hash its input instead of sorting, because hashing preserves order
Sort only the smallest key and discard the rest
Run external sorting on its own data
Always gather all partitions onto one machine for sorting
questions.explanation: The lecture distributes the work and then runs external sorting independently on each machine.

questions.prompt: Node A holds keys <100 and node B holds keys ≥100; both are sorted. How can a global ascending order be produced?
options: Concatenate B's output before A's
Interleave tuples from A and B arbitrarily
Keep only the output of the partition with larger keys
Concatenate A's output before B's
questions.explanation: Ordered, non-overlapping ranges allow concatenation in boundary order.

questions.prompt: If tuples are distributed round-robin and then sorted locally, does concatenating the nodes' outputs guarantee global order?
options: No, the nodes' key domains can interleave
Yes, local sorting automatically establishes key boundaries between nodes
Yes, provided every node has the same number of tuples
Yes, because round-robin keeps all small keys at the first node
questions.explanation: Local sorting does not order arbitrary partitions relative to one another; range partitioning or an additional merge is needed.

questions.prompt: What is the risk if one range contains 90% of the tuples?
options: Increasing the number of ranges automatically guarantees equal sorting times
Sorting at that node becomes a bottleneck
The local sort becomes incorrect solely because the distribution is skewed
External sorting works only when all partitions have the same size
questions.explanation: Sorting remains correct, but skew reduces parallelism; suitable range boundaries are needed to balance the load.

questions.prompt: How must the two relations be range-partitioned?
options: On the join key, with arbitrary independent boundaries for each table
On any sort column, even if it is not the join key
On the join key using the same ranges
Round-robin with the same number of partitions is always sufficient
questions.explanation: The same key and boundaries ensure that matching pairs reach the same node.

questions.prompt: R is split at 100 and S at 50, then corresponding nodes perform local joins. What problem can occur?
options: Every pair remains co-located merely because both tables use id
Local sorting automatically fixes placement mismatches between nodes
Different boundaries affect only output order and cannot cause missed pairs
Tuples with the same key 75 can be on different nodes
questions.explanation: Different boundaries break co-location; partitioning on the same column alone is insufficient.

questions.prompt: After compatible range partitioning, which join runs at each machine?
options: An independent sort-merge join
A Cartesian product without applying the join condition
Simple concatenation of the two sorted relations
A mandatory broadcast of every partition to every node
questions.explanation: Each node sorts and merges its relevant data using the local algorithm.

questions.prompt: How do the distribution steps differ for parallel hash join and sort-merge join in the slides?
options: Hash join uses the join key, but sort-merge join does not need it
Hash partitioning on the key versus range partitioning on the key
Both require round-robin distribution
Sort-merge join always avoids all network-transfer costs
questions.explanation: Both require matching keys to be co-located, but they use hash and range partitioning respectively.

questions.prompt: If all tuples have the same join key, does adding ranges automatically divide them evenly for local joins?
options: Yes, every range automatically receives equal tuple counts even when keys are equal
Yes, disjoint ranges all contain the same hot key
No, they must still be handled according to the co-location rules
Yes, local sorting automatically redistributes tuples to less busy nodes
questions.explanation: Range partitioning does not automatically solve the hot-key problem; distributing matching pairs across nodes requires an additional strategy.

questions.prompt: What is the central principle for a correct distributed join?
options: Preserve input locations even when matching pairs are on different nodes
It is enough for the tables to have the same number of partitions
It is enough for all nodes to know the join key's name
Bring matching tuples together at the same processing location
questions.explanation: Every matching pair must meet; the partitioning scheme determines how much communication is needed.

questions.prompt: Why is gathering both tables onto one node usually a naive approach?
options: It incurs network-transfer costs and loses parallelism
A single node cannot execute a logically correct join
Every distributed join must broadcast entire tables
Centralizing data always eliminates all local I/O
questions.explanation: A local join can still be correct, but centralizing all inputs sacrifices the benefits of distributed processing.

questions.prompt: What directly affects the efficiency of a distributed join?
options: Only table sizes; tuple locations have no effect
The inputs' existing partitioning schemes
Only the number of CPUs, without considering network costs
Only the result count, without considering input movement
questions.explanation: Partitioning determines whether matching pairs are already on the same node or need to be moved.

questions.prompt: Once matching tuples are on the same node, is an entirely new family of join algorithms required?
options: Yes, local hash join cannot be used after repartitioning
Yes, only nested-loop joins can run at each node
No, the local join algorithms already studied can be used
No, because co-location completely replaces join-condition checks
questions.explanation: The lecture reuses conventional join algorithms after resolving data placement.

questions.prompt: Two plans produce the same correct result. Which cost can still differ substantially?
options: The meaning of key equality automatically changes between nodes
The correct number of rows must change with the movement algorithm
The number of logical replicas in the result must increase with the machine count
The amount of data transferred between nodes
questions.explanation: Input placement and movement strategies can lead to very different network costs.

questions.prompt: In Scenario #1, what is assumed about one input table?
options: It is replicated at every node
It exists only at the coordinator and has not yet been distributed
It is partitioned across nodes using a different key
Each node holds only a disjoint subset
questions.explanation: Table S is already replicated, so every node has all of S to join with its local portion of R.

questions.prompt: What join does each node perform in Scenario #1?
options: The whole of R with the whole of S at every node, followed by concatenation of all results
Its local portion of R with a complete copy of S
Its local R with an arbitrary portion of S, regardless of keys
Only R tuples that have already matched at another node
questions.explanation: R is divided among nodes and every node has all of S; each portion of R contributes its corresponding results.

questions.prompt: According to the diagram, where do results go after the local joins?
options: Only one node's result is retained because S is replicated
They are broadcast again to repeat the same join
To the coordinator for combination
They must pass through DISTINCT to remove all rows with equal values
questions.explanation: The coordinator combines the results; it does not change the input tables.

questions.prompt: Why is there no need to broadcast S again at join time if valid replicas already exist?
options: The tables have equal row counts, so no movement is needed
The join reads only R and no longer needs S
The coordinator can infer all of S from R's keys
Every node already has all of S
questions.explanation: The benefit comes from existing replication, not from ignoring one of the join's inputs.

questions.prompt: R has disjoint partitions and S is replicated. How can duplicate computation caused by replicas be avoided?
options: Each node joins only the portion of R it owns with S
Every node joins all of R with S, then all results are concatenated
Automatically delete all equal-valued rows even when the query has no DISTINCT
Perform the join at only one node while R remains distributed
questions.explanation: Dividing R ensures each logical pair is processed in the right place; applying DISTINCT arbitrarily can violate bag semantics.

questions.prompt: What enables local joins in Scenario #2?
options: Both tables have the same partition count but arbitrary key mappings
R and S are co-partitioned on the join key
R is partitioned by name and S by val
Each node knows only the other table's metadata
questions.explanation: The diagram uses the same id ranges for both tables at each node.

questions.prompt: P1 holds ids 1–100 for both R and S. Where is a pair with key 70 processed?
options: P2, because a key must move to another node before joining
Both P1 and P2 must produce the same result pair
P1
The coordinator must receive both complete tables before processing
questions.explanation: The tuples with key 70 are both at P1 because the tables are co-partitioned.

questions.prompt: Must entire tables be transferred before the join in this configuration?
options: Yes, every distributed join must gather its inputs onto one machine
Yes, both R and S must always be broadcast to every node
There is no need to combine the nodes' results after the join
No, matching pairs are already co-located
questions.explanation: Compatible placement avoids transferring inputs for the join; results may still need to be sent elsewhere.

questions.prompt: Is saying that both tables are partitioned by id enough to guarantee local joins?
options: No, the mappings from id values to nodes must be compatible
Yes, even if the same id maps to different nodes
Yes, if partition counts match but range boundaries differ
No, because every local join requires a fully replicated table
questions.explanation: The same key with different hash mappings or range boundaries can put matching tuples on different nodes.

questions.prompt: What does the coalescing step in the diagram do?
options: Redistribute all inputs even though they are already co-partitioned
Gather the nodes' join results
Apply DISTINCT to every result regardless of the SQL query
Change the join condition to fit the existing partitions
questions.explanation: Results from individual partitions are combined into the global query result.

questions.prompt: R and S have incompatible partitioning, S is small, and each worker can hold S. Which redistribution strategy can enable local joins?
options: Broadcast the larger table because the smaller table is less worth moving
Join the existing partitions immediately and treat that as the complete result
Broadcast S to the nodes
Send only S's schema instead of its data
questions.explanation: Broadcast S so each worker joins its own R partition against the complete S. Equal keys can then meet without moving all of R. The memory and update costs of copying S still matter.

questions.prompt: Why does the size of S matter for a broadcast join?
options: A small table does not need its join condition checked
A small table always has only one key value
Broadcasting sends only one copy regardless of the number of nodes
S must be sent to multiple nodes
questions.explanation: Multiplying transfer costs by the number of nodes can make broadcasting a large table very expensive.

questions.prompt: After S is broadcast, what does each node join?
options: Its local R with all of S
Its local R with only the original portion of S from before the broadcast
All of R with all of S at every node, followed by concatenation of all results
Only portions of S across nodes, without reading R
questions.explanation: Broadcasting compensates for S originally being partitioned by val rather than id.

questions.prompt: What is the main difference between Scenario #3 and Scenario #1?
options: Scenario #1 always requires both tables to be shuffled
Complete copies of S are created through data transfer during execution
Scenario #3 needs no network transfer before the join
Scenario #1 requires co-partitioned tables rather than replication
questions.explanation: #1 already has replicas; #3 must broadcast the small table from its initial placement.

questions.prompt: If S is no longer small, which decision is reasonable?
options: Continue broadcasting because table size does not affect cost
Discard tuples exceeding RAM capacity to keep broadcasting cheap
Re-evaluate the costs of broadcasting versus repartitioning
Join only part of S to avoid transferring too much data
questions.explanation: Broadcast costs must be considered; repartitioning is an alternative when sending many copies becomes too expensive.

questions.prompt: When neither R nor S is partitioned on the join key, what does Scenario #4 do?
options: Join the existing partitions even though their partition keys are unrelated to the join
Broadcast only column names, then join locally
Merely sort each existing partition to guarantee co-location
Reshuffle both tables on the join key
questions.explanation: Both inputs are moved to an id-based layout so matching pairs can be joined locally.

questions.prompt: R is initially partitioned by name and S by val, but they join on id. What is the goal of shuffling?
options: Bring tuples with the same id in both tables to the same node
Change the ON condition to name=val to match the layout
Sort locally by id while never moving any tuples
Create copies of join results before processing the inputs
questions.explanation: The query condition stays unchanged; only the physical placement changes.

questions.prompt: According to the diagram, which processing step follows the reshuffle?
options: Simply concatenate R and S because they now have the same partition key
Perform local joins, then gather the results
Match only unequal keys to avoid duplicates
Gather metadata instead of join results
questions.explanation: The diagram proceeds from repartitioning to joins at the nodes and then to combining results.

questions.prompt: Compared with #2, which cost is more apparent in #4?
options: A mandatory change to the logical result set
Having to abandon local joins after moving data
Transferring inputs to achieve co-partitioning
Reducing the number of logical tuples by removing duplicate keys
questions.explanation: #2 already has compatible placement; #4 pays a shuffle cost to create similar conditions.

questions.prompt: Does reshuffling mean that every node always receives a complete copy of both tables?
options: Yes, shuffling always means broadcasting both tables
Yes, every tuple must be stored permanently at every node
No, because shuffling changes only metadata and never transfers tuples
No, tuples are routed to their respective destination partitions
questions.explanation: Unlike broadcasting, repartitioning divides data by key; the illustration shows different id ranges.

questions.prompt: Which optimizations from a single-node system still apply in a distributed system?
options: Predicate pushdown, early projection, and join-order selection
Only join-order selection; predicate pushdown no longer works
Always postponing filters until after all data is transferred
Always projecting away join keys before distribution
questions.explanation: Logical optimizations remain useful and can also reduce the amount of data sent over the network.

questions.prompt: Besides local costs, what must the optimizer account for?
options: Only local I/O, because network transfers are always free
Data location and network costs
Only total CPU use, regardless of where data resides
Only the number of partitions, ignoring transferred data volume
questions.explanation: Location determines which data must move; transfer time or volume is a crucial cost.

questions.prompt: Two parallel branches take 500 ms and 300 ms. Ignoring overhead, how long does the overall execution take?
options: 300 ms
400 ms
500 ms
800 ms
questions.explanation: Execution must wait for the slower branch; the sum of 800 ms represents total work, not elapsed time when the branches run concurrently.

questions.prompt: What is the benefit of projecting away unnecessary columns before a shuffle?
options: It always reduces the tuple count to one
It allows required join keys to be removed while preserving correctness
It eliminates all transfer costs even when tuples still need to be sent
It reduces the bytes transferred while retaining columns needed by the query
questions.explanation: Projection reduces tuple width; required columns must remain to preserve the query's semantics.

questions.prompt: Why is load balancing important for a distributed plan?
options: One overloaded node can determine the completion time
Overall runtime equals the fastest node's runtime
All nodes automatically take the same time even when their data volumes differ
Adding nodes guarantees there are no remaining bottlenecks
questions.explanation: Skew creates bottlenecks; adding nodes does not automatically remove the uneven work on a slow node.
